criteria.name: Introduction: mission concept and rationale - Include the following required information: • What is the spacecraft's primary mission? • Why is the mission needed? • How many spacecraft are used and why? • Who are the users (operator and customers)?
criteria.reasoning: Primary mission (fluid-lensing reef monitoring), rationale (bleaching statistics), single-spacecraft justification, and users/funding (CSIRO, BOM, government/university) all addressed with cited literature. Detail is good though user discussion is somewhat brief.

evidence.quote: Thus, only one satellite is required. This also just allows for simplicity in communications, reduces cost
The proposed satellite would likely be used by governmental and science agencies (e.g. CSIRO, BOM)

criteria.name: Main body: mission design - Present a summary of the mission design using software and/or hand calculations as appropriate - Include relevant screenshots and software files (in the main body of the report and/or appendix) - Include the following information: • Where it will launch from, and using which launch vehicle? Why did you choose this option? • What type of orbit will you use? What are its characteristics and orbital elements? • Will you need to perform any orbital maneuvers? • Which ground control facilities will you use? • How often will your spacecraft be able to communicate with ground control? • How long will the mission last, and what are your plans for EOL?
criteria.reasoning: All major requirements addressed: launch site/vehicle with rationale, SSO with full COE table, manoeuvres (none until EOL), ground station selection logic, STK access report quantifying comms frequency, 5-year duration and drag-sail EOL. Supported by STK screenshots and inclination plot. Minor logic errors (altitude/resolution statement) prevent top mark.

technical_issues.issue: States 'A very high altitude would yield low resolution images which is also desirable' – contradicts the design logic; low resolution is undesirable.
Wikipedia (2021 in spaceflight) cited as reference [6], which the task explicitly disallows as a proper source.
Claim that RAAN of 27.33° 'indicates the location of the launch facility' is dubious; RAAN is set by launch time/window, not directly by site.
Assertion that the facility 'will be able to receive all new data from the previous period' is unsupported by any link-budget or data-rate analysis.
Suggests lifespan 'may be lengthened by the addition of solar panels' – solar panels are standard, not an EOL-extension mechanism; also text garbled around drag sail description.

overall: A well-structured, mostly comprehensive mission design with good STK evidence covering all major space-segment requirements. Weakened by a few technical logic errors, unnumbered figures/tables, bare-URL referencing including Wikipedia, and no evidence of attached software files.

feedback.summary: Your Great Barrier Reef fluid-lensing mission design is well structured and addresses all major space-segment requirements, supported by STK evidence and hand calculations. To reach the top band, fix technical logic slips (altitude/resolution, RAAN claim), support the ground-contact data claim with analysis, attach your software files, and improve figure/table labelling and referencing.
next_steps: Attach your STK scenario/software files (appendix or submission folder) so your simulation evidence is fully verifiable.
Number all figures (e.g. Figure 1) and label all tables with captions, and make heading formatting consistent throughout.
Replace Wikipedia and bare URLs with proper citations to primary sources (e.g. Vega E datasheets, CSIRO/BOM publications) in a consistently formatted reference list.
Correct the technical logic errors: the altitude/resolution statement, the RAAN–launch-site claim, and the solar-panel lifespan comment; clarify the drag sail description.
Add a link-budget or data-rate analysis to substantiate the claim that the ground station receives all data between passes, and quantify mission outcomes in the conclusion.

criteria.C1: Strong work: your introduction clearly states the primary mission (fluid-lensing reef monitoring), justifies a single satellite for simplicity and cost, and identifies users (CSIRO, BOM, government/university) with cited literature. To reach the very top of the band, expand the user discussion—detail how each user accesses and applies the imagery, and cite specific funding or program examples.
criteria.C2: Excellent coverage: Kourou/Vega E with rationale, a full COE table for your 600 km SSO, a justified no-manoeuvre-until-EOL plan, Mt Pleasant ground station with a quantified STK access report (~10 min average contact), and a 5-year duration with drag-sail EOL, all evidenced by STK screenshots and your inclination plot. The top band requires error-free logic: fix the 'low resolution is desirable' contradiction, the RAAN/launch-site claim, and support the 'all data received' assertion with a link-budget or data-rate calculation. Also attach your software files.
criteria.C3: Your conclusions are specific and evidence-based, including honest risk acknowledgment about the unbuilt Vega E and alternatives—good practice. To strengthen this, quantify outcomes (e.g. revisit coverage achieved, data volumes downlinked) and briefly state whether the mission meets its stated reef-monitoring objectives.
criteria.C4: Your report has a clear structure with an executive summary and logical sections, but presentation holds you back: figures lack numbers, tables are unlabelled, headings are inconsistently formatted, and there are grammar slips ('a Earth observation', 'It's first launch', 'for the purposed of'). The bibliography uses bare URLs including Wikipedia, which is not an acceptable source. Number/label all figures and tables, proofread carefully, and adopt a consistent citation style (e.g. IEEE) matching in-text citations to the reference list.
